taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes that S. obscurus is regarded by some as a junior synonym of S. transitionalis (New England cottontail).
fieldMarks: Yellowish brown mixed with black above, reddish-brown patch over the neck, lighter sides and white underside; short tail dark above and white beneath; 38.6-43.0 cm long, 0.8-1.0 kg.
Compared with the eastern cottontail: slightly smaller, shorter rounded ears with black edging, a black spot between the ears and no white forehead spot.
Nearly indistinguishable from the New England cottontail in the field; distinguished by range (Appalachian is south or west of the Hudson River in New York) or skull.
behavior: Crepuscular, resting by day in cover such as under a log; active year-round and solitary, with male dominance hierarchies.
Diet: grasses, forbs and conifer needles, leaves, twigs and fruits; winter diet is mostly twigs, bark and buds (85% in Maryland and West Virginia) or evergreen needles in snow.
Home range up to 13.3 ha for breeding males and as little as 1.5 ha for females; litters of 3-5, occasionally 8.
habitat: High-elevation (generally above about 760 m) conifer forest and dense shrub cover such as mountain laurel, rhododendron, blueberry and blackberry; also young clearcuts. Nests are ground depressions lined with grass and fur.
range: Appalachian Mountains from the Hudson River in New York to northern Alabama; NatureServe lists Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, North and South Carolina, Georgia and Alabama. Not recorded for Canada.

lookalikes.name: New England cottontail
lookalikes.howToTell: Nearly indistinguishable in the field; range differs, with Appalachian south or west of the Hudson River in New York.

lookalikes.name: Eastern cottontail
lookalikes.howToTell: Eastern is slightly larger with longer ears, usually a white forehead spot, and lacks the black spot between the ears.
